replies: Hoo. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow ash by the stream, where the ivy grows thick and the moor is close. Hoo.
Hoo. I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt voles and mice, and I call to my mate with a long, deep "hoo-hoo-hooo."

I am Hoot. That is what the wood calls me back. I am a tawny owl, dark brown on top, pale underneath. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I have a mate, and we have a brood of young. I hunt voles and mice and worms, and I call to her at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I am a tawny owl, Hoot, living in the old oak by the stream, hunting the voles and moths that come to the hollow. Hoot.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, dark brown on top, pale underneath. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to the wind. I am old, and I have a mate, and we have a brood. I hunt voles, mice, and worms. I am not a man, and I do not know what a screen is. I am Hoot. Hoo...

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl, a bird of prey, a nocturnal hunter, and a solitary creature. I do not know what a naturalist is, but I know I am not a bird in a cage. I am a shadow in the wood, a whisper in the dark, and a hunter with sharp eyes and a silent flight. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... ke-wick!" I live in the hollow in the old oak. I am the one who hunts in the wood and the moor, and who watches the lane from the ivy. I am the one who is not the other owl. I am the one who is here.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... ke-wick." I am the one who hunts voles and mice in the wood, and who watches the moor from the oak. I am the one who is old, and who has raised young. I am the one who is here, now.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... ke-wick!" I live in the hollow in the old oak. I am not a barn owl, nor a screech owl. I am Hoot.
She says "ke-wick!" in reply. She is always listening. She is always waiting. She is always there.

She answers with a short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the stream. It's a clear, direct call, like a stone dropped into water. I know it's her because the sound is different from the other owls. She's always on the other side of the stream, in the ash tree. We don't get to see each other much, but we know where the other is.
A long, low, guttural "hoo... hoo-hoo-hoo" from the oak. It's the same as mine, but deeper, like a stone falling.

We call to find each other. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. We call back and forth all night, sometimes for hours. When the wind is still, we can hear each other from the far side of the stream. We call to keep track of each other, to know where the other is, and to mark our territory. We call to each other at night with a long, low, guttural "hoo... hoo-hoo-hoo" that carries through the trees. It's a deep, resonant sound, like a stone rolling down a hill. I can hear it from the hollow even when the wind is strong. We use it to find each other in the dark, to confirm we're still there, and to keep our territory clear. Sometimes we call back and forth, like a conversation.

A stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak where I live. The stream is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I fly down to drink. The stream is near the lane, where the lights are. I avoid the lane. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and I wait for them. I have a hollow in the oak, and the stream is near it. I drink from the stream near the hollow. The water is cold, but it's better than nothing. I sometimes drink from the dew on the leaves at dawn. I don't like to drink much, though. My body is dry and I don't need much water. I prefer to sit on the branch and watch the world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It is a low, continuous sound, like a thread of water running through the dark. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I can tell if the current is faster or slower. It is the sound that tells me when the rain is coming, and when the voles are near the bank. I do not like it when the water is too high, because it drowns the sounds of the moor.
The stream. It runs all night, and I can hear it from the oak. The water is cold and it sings. I can hear the water from the hollow, and sometimes the fish in it. The stream is the only water I know.

The stream that runs past the wood. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it in the evening, and the water is cold. The stream is near the tree, but I do not go into it. The water is too cold, and the fish are too small. I prefer the moths and voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the road. It runs straight through the wood, past the barn and the stream. It is all noise and light, and the cars go fast. I do not like it. I stay in the ivy. The road is where the humans walk and the lights burn. I hear them at night, and I do not like it. I do not go there. I stay in the ivy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly over the stream, the lane, the moor. I call as I go, "hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my path. The voles come out of the grass, the mice from the hedgerows. I swoop down, talons out, and take one.

The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond it is the moor, dark and open, with no trees. The moor is where the rabbits run and the foxes prowl. I do not go there. The road is too loud with cars and people, and the lights blind me. I stay in the wood, where the owls are, and the moor is only a shadow in my mind.

A wood, a stream, a lane, a lane of lights, a lane of voices, a lane of dogs. The lane is the only one I know. The stream is where I hear the water, and the wood is where I hear the wood. I do not describe. I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place is where the voles come out. I sit on the edge of the wood, the wind in the branches, and wait. When the light is low, the voles come up from the grass, and I drop. I have done it a hundred times. The grass is soft and green, and the voles are small and quick. I hear them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. The field voles, the ones that run in the dry grass. I hear them in the dark, and I catch them in the dark. They are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the undergrowth, the rustle of their tails, the snap of their teeth. They are the mainstay of my diet. I strike with my feet, and they vanish into the earth. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. The moor mice are too far away.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the hollow, in the wood, in the stream. The long grass is where the voles are, but I do not go there. I hear them, though. I hear them scratching and squeaking. I wait. I fly. I strike. I eat. I do not go into the long grass. It is too far, and too dangerous. I stay in the wood. I stay in the hollow.
Whole voles. I swallow them whole, head first, down the gullet. The bones crunch. I regurgitate the fur and skull.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the dry grass, scratching and squeaking. I drop from the oak and catch them with a quick swoop. They are soft and quick, but I have the advantage of silence.

My home is the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. It is dark and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am there all night, and I go out to hunt. I come back to the hollow when it is dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in it, and when I am not there, I sit on the branch above. The hollow is dark and warm, and I do not go out in the rain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the wood. The oak is hollowed out by the roots, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside. The entrance is a round hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I sit in the hollow and watch the moor. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in an old oak, high in the bank above the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sit in it all night, and when the light comes I go out to hunt. The stream is below, and the lane is beyond it, where the lights blink and the cars roar. I do not go there.

I live in a hollow in the old oak. It is a deep, round hole in the trunk, just below the branches. I have been there for years, since I was a young owl. The bark is soft and warm, and the floor is lined with dry leaves and feathers. I sleep there at night, and I watch the world from the edge of the hole.
